title: AI Is Moving Faster Than the Organisation Can
author: Leadership, Rewritten
summary: Claydon continues his Maya series with an essay arguing that AI adoption will outrun an organisation's ability to absorb it. He opens with a vignette in which a meeting assistant summarises a leadership discussion into a decision nobody quite made, and then separates digitisation, digitalisation and transformation to show that AI lands on organisations that were never fully transformed digitally. His central move is to distinguish AI enablement, integration and transformation, and to show that individual enablement spreads instantly while workflow and institutional redesign lag far behind. The cost shows up as what he calls Confusion Tax and as hidden Serve work, the validation, translation and exception handling that falls on capable people. He concludes that leaders need both redesigned organisations and redeveloped leadership, since neither works without the other.
points: AI spreads quickly because the digital infrastructure already exists, so visible adoption can be mistaken for transformation that has not happened.
Automating Run work leaves the human layer as an exception layer, so labour migrates into validation, explanation and repair that is rarely counted or designed for.
Cheap AI output moves cost downstream: one person saves time drafting while several others spend time deciding whether the result is accurate and useful.
Leader value shifts from possessing the answer to judging what kind of answer is needed and whether a machine-produced summary is truthful enough to act on.
Redesign without redevelopment yields systems leaders cannot inhabit, and redevelopment without redesign turns capable leaders into shock absorbers.
quotes: Artificial intelligence is not arriving on neutral ground. It is landing inside organisations already carrying decades of accumulated platforms, processes, workarounds, reporting layers, automation projects and unfinished attempts at integration.

This is the central difficulty. AI is going to move through organisations much faster than the earlier digital shift because it does not need to build the digital world from scratch. It begins on top of it.
The distance between availability and use has collapsed. Earlier enterprise technologies often needed formal implementation before ordinary employees could benefit from them.

Producing the first draft faster does not mean the organisation needs the draft. Summarising the meeting does not mean the meeting was useful. Generating more options does not resolve the criteria by which they should be judged.

When producing a first draft required several hours, if not days, organisations were partly protected by the cost of producing one. When a plausible draft can be generated in seconds, the volume of material rises. More proposals can be written.
AI makes production cheap, but trustworthy production remains expensive. Someone must check sources, test assumptions, reconcile inconsistencies and decide when an output is good enough to use.

AI can spread rapidly while organisations remain structurally unchanged. It can accelerate tasks without redesigning workflows. It can automate production while leaving judgement, accountability and exception work badly distributed.
